proposals.before: At the time the headquarters Registrar Zong Xie also had lofty tastes; Daogui and both men alike looked to one another for a life beyond official business.
proposals.after: At the time the headquarters Registrar Zong Xie also had lofty tastes; Daogui counted on both men alike for companionship beyond official business.
proposals.reason: Chinese 道規並以事外相期 makes Daogui the subject who looked to Jinghong and Zong Xie for extra-official companionship, not an equal three-way looking among all three.

proposals.before: The late Palace Attendant, Left Grand Master of the Palace, and Jinghong, who held the privilege of an office equal to the Three Excellencies, had a spirit unassuming and plain and a vision lofty and far-reaching. His virtue reached the capital's gate-towers, his Way enriched hill and garden alike.
proposals.after: The late Palace Attendant, Left Grand Master of the Palace with the privilege of an office equal to the Three Excellencies, Jinghong, had a spirit unassuming and plain and a vision lofty and far-reaching. His virtue reached the capital's gate-towers; his Way enriched hill and garden alike.
proposals.reason: Chinese lists three offices then the name 敬弘; the English splits Jinghong off as if a separate conjunct from 開府儀同三司.

proposals.before: The late Palace Attendant, Left Grand Master of the Palace, and Jinghong, who held the privilege of an office equal to the Three Excellencies, had a spirit and bearing unassuming and plain, understanding and scope lofty and steep; his virtue spread to the gate-towers of the capital, his Way enriched hill and garden.
proposals.after: The late Palace Attendant, Left Grand Master of the Palace, and holder of the privilege of an office equal to the Three Excellencies, Jinghong, had a spirit and bearing unassuming and plain, understanding and scope lofty and steep; his virtue spread to the gate-towers of the capital, his Way enriched hill and garden.
proposals.reason: The literal English likewise inserts an 'and' that makes Jinghong a fourth item instead of the person who held 開府儀同三司.

proposals.before: Jinghong was short in stature, yet in sitting and rising he was perfectly upright. Huan Xuan called him "the eight formations of go."
proposals.after: Jinghong was short in stature, yet in sitting and rising he was perfectly upright. Huan Xuan called him "the eight formations of tanqi."
proposals.reason: 彈棊 is the game tanqi (pellet chess), not go (圍棋); the epithet is mistranslated.

proposals.before: Jinghong's form was short and small, yet in sitting and rising he was upright and square. Huan Xuan called him "the eight formations of go."
proposals.after: Jinghong's form was short and small, yet in sitting and rising he was upright and square. Huan Xuan called him "the eight formations of tanqi."
proposals.reason: 彈棊 is tanqi, not go; the literal field repeats the same error.

proposals.before: Xu Xiu of Donghai, He Tan of Lujiang, Huang Hui, Sun Zichang and Wang Yanxiu of Taiyuan, Kong Huixuan of Lu Commandery, and others all admired the Way and came to study; this was called the Southern School.
proposals.after: Xu Xiu of Donghai, He Tan of Lujiang, Huang Hui, Xun Zihua of Yingchuan, Sun Zongchang and Wang Yanxiu of Taiyuan, Kong Huixuan of Lu Commandery, and others all admired the Way and came to study; this was called the Southern School.
proposals.reason: Chinese lists 潁川荀子華 before the Taiyuan names and writes 孫宗昌; the idiomatic English omits Xun Zihua of Yingchuan and misreads 宗 as Zi.

proposals.before: Xu Xiu of Donghai, He Tan of Lujiang, Huang Hui, Sun Zichang and Wang Yanxiu of Taiyuan, Kong Huixuan of Lu Commandery, and others all admired the Way and came to study; this was called the Southern School.
proposals.after: Xu Xiu of Donghai, He Tan of Lujiang, Huang Hui, Xun Zihua of Yingchuan, Sun Zongchang and Wang Yanxiu of Taiyuan, Kong Huixuan of Lu Commandery, and others all admired the Way and came to study; this was called the Southern School.
proposals.reason: Literal English likewise drops 潁川荀子華 and renders 孫宗昌 as Sun Zichang.

proposals.before: When Emperor Shaodi came to the throne, Shangzhi became Advisory Army Aide on the Household Cavalry staff of the Prince of Luling, Yizhen.
proposals.after: When Emperor Shaodi came to the throne, Shangzhi became Advisory Army Aide to the Prince of Luling, Yizhen, as General of Chariots and Cavalry.
proposals.reason: 車騎 here is the prince's generalship 車騎將軍, not the Household Cavalry.

proposals.before: If limited to four or five zhu, the inscriptions are all ancient seal script, which common people do not recognize; moreover some are worn away and especially hard to distinguish. Public and private will be thrown into confusion and lawsuits will surely arise—this is his deepest doubt.
proposals.after: If limited to four or five zhu, the inscriptions are all ancient seal script, which those in humble service do not recognize; moreover some are worn away and especially hard to distinguish. Public and private will be thrown into confusion and lawsuits will surely arise—this is the deepest of these doubts.
proposals.reason: 下走 is the memorialist's humble self-reference; 其深疑 is the doubt about the proposal, not a third-person 'his'.

proposals.before: In the twenty-ninth year he retired and at Fang Mountain wrote a Rhapsody on Retirement to declare what he upheld, but commentators all said Shangzhi could not hold firm to his resolve. Yuan Shu, Left Commander of the Heir Apparent's Guard, wrote to him: "Yesterday I sent inquiry and learned that you, sir, have hidden your will in mountain fields. Though one says the rites of age should be followed, this is hard to esteem so highly. Bi Shu, Ban Chao, Bing, and Wei would shine in former records; Gong, Gong, Shan, and Wei would sink in shame in past chapters.
proposals.after: In the twenty-ninth year he retired and at Fang Mountain wrote a Rhapsody on Retirement to declare what he upheld, but commentators all said Shangzhi could not hold firm to his resolve. Yuan Shu, Left Commander of the Heir Apparent's Guard, wrote to him: "Yesterday I sent inquiry and learned that you, sir, have hidden your will in mountain fields. Though one says the rites of age should be followed, this is hard to esteem so highly. Shu, Ban, Bing, and Wei would then share excellence in former records; Gong, Gong, Shan, and Wei would sink in shame in past chapters.
proposals.reason: 疎 is Shu, not Bi Shu; 俾 marks a comparative wish, not that Ban Chao himself would shine in Yuanjia.

proposals.before: Shangzhi's residence was beside Nanjian Temple, hence the letter says 'southern bank'—as in the Mao Ode's 'To gather duckweed, on the southern stream's bank.'"
proposals.after: Shangzhi's residence was beside Nanjian Temple, hence the letter says 'southern bank'—as in the Mao Ode's 'To gather duckweed, on the southern stream's bank.'
proposals.reason: Stray extra closing quotation mark after the ode citation.

proposals.before: Edicts earnestly urged him. The emperor also sent an edict to the Prince of Jiangxia, Yigong, saying, "Court worthies are few today, and Yang and Meng have not yet been permitted to retire. Shangzhi's appointment and favor are special—is it then not fitting to grant his request?"
proposals.after: Edicts earnestly urged him. The emperor also sent an edict to the Prince of Jiangxia, Yigong, saying, "Court worthies are few today, and Yang and Meng have not yet been permitted to retire. Shangzhi's appointment and favor are special—so it is not yet fitting to grant his request, is it?"
proposals.reason: After noting Yang and Meng were refused, 未宜申許邪 rhetorically confirms Shangzhi should not yet be allowed to retire.

proposals.before: His son Shao married the sixteenth daughter of Emperor Taizu, the Princess of Nan Commandery; his daughter married the Prince of Pengcheng, Yikang, and the Lamented Prince of Baling, Xiuruo.
proposals.after: His son Shao married the sixteenth daughter of Emperor Taizu, the Princess of Nan Commandery; his daughters married the Prince of Pengcheng, Yikang, and the Lamented Prince of Baling, Xiuruo.
proposals.reason: 女適甲、乙 records two princely marriages and should be plural daughters.

proposals.before: Qingzhi repeatedly declined ennoblement; the court earnestly urged him with great sincerity. Shangzhi said to him, "The sovereign empties his mind and sits sidewise—how could you firmly decline?"
proposals.after: Qingzhi repeatedly declined ennoblement; the court earnestly urged him with great sincerity. Shangzhi said to him, "The sovereign opens his mind and keeps a seat at his side—how could you firmly decline?"
proposals.reason: 側席 describes the ruler leaving a place at his side for a worthy, not sitting 'sidewise'; the current phrasing obscures the idiom.

proposals.before: He was on good terms with Wang Wei of Langye. When Youzhi died, Wei wrote to Yan: "I and the Administrator of Yixing only regret that we knew each other late; I always thought that a gentleman understood me.
proposals.after: Youzhi was on good terms with Wang Wei of Langye. When Youzhi died, Wei wrote to Yan: "I and the Administrator of Yixing only regret that we knew each other late; I always thought that a gentleman understood me.
proposals.reason: The silent Chinese subject of 與琅邪王微相善 continues 悠之 from the previous sentence; a generic He conceals that the friendship belongs to Youzhi, not Shangzhi or Yan.
